lessons.title: The ESOP Pool: Why Investors Want It Created Before They Invest

children.text: Deep in most term sheets is a line that reads something like "a 10% employee option pool will be created prior to closing, on a fully diluted basis". It looks administrative. It is one of the most expensive sentences in the document, and it is where a headline valuation quietly shrinks. This lesson shows you exactly how much it costs, why investors ask for it, and how to negotiate the size with something better than arguments.

body.text: A pre-money option pool is a price cut dressed as good governance. The investor still gets the percentage they asked for, the employees get their shares, and the entire cost lands on the people who were already shareholders.

children.text: What the Pool Is

markDefs.definition: A block of shares reserved for grants to employees under an employee stock option plan. The shares are set aside now and issued as employees exercise their options later.
A share count that includes everything convertible into equity: issued shares, the whole option pool whether granted or not, and outstanding convertible instruments.

children.text: An
ESOP pool
is a reserved block of shares for employees, approved by the board and by shareholders through a special resolution, and administered under a written plan. Investors always measure it on a
fully diluted
basis, which means the whole pool counts against ownership from day one, even the part that has not been granted to anyone.
The Same Round, Two Places to Put the Pool

An illustrative Chennai company has 70,00,000 shares held by its founders. An investor offers ₹5 crore at a ₹20 crore pre-money valuation, taking 20%, and wants a 10% option pool. Where that pool sits changes everything.

body.caption: ₹5 crore at ₹20 crore pre-money, with a 10% pool created two different ways

children.text: Read the bottom row again. In the pre-money version the investor pays ₹25 a share. In the post-money version the same ₹5 crore buys shares at ₹28.57. The valuation on the term sheet says ₹20 crore either way, but the price actually paid is not the same.

body.caption: A ₹20 crore pre-money valuation with a 10% pre-money pool is really ₹17.5 crore

stats.label: Effective pre-money
stats.context: What the founders are really being paid, after the pool

body.title: What is the real pre-money?
body.prompt: Using the pre-money pool version above, the investor pays ₹25 per share and the founders held 70,00,000 shares before the round. What is the effective pre-money valuation, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: 70,00,000 × ₹25 = ₹17,50,00,000, which is ₹17.5 crore, not the ₹20 crore printed on the term sheet. The missing ₹2.5 crore is the pool, and the founders paid for all of it. This is why experienced founders compare offers on price per share, never on the headline valuation.

body.text: Investors are not being sneaky, they are being consistent. Their argument is that the company needs those employees to deliver the plan they are funding, so the cost of hiring them belongs to the value of the business as it stands today. That argument is reasonable. It is also negotiable, and the negotiation is about size, not principle.

children.text: Negotiate the Size With a Hiring Plan

"15% is standard" is not an argument, it is a habit. The only credible response is a bottom-up plan showing who you will hire over the next 18 months and what each grant needs to be. Investors accept this, because it is the same reasoning they used.

body.caption: A bottom-up pool build for the next 18 months

children.text: Going from a 12% pool to 8% on the Chennai example above is worth roughly 4% of the company. At a ₹25 crore post-money valuation that is ₹1 crore of founder value, recovered by spending an afternoon building a hiring table.

body.title: Two ways to answer "we need a 15% pool"

columns.label: What loses the argument
points: Agreeing to 15% and planning to negotiate it later
Treating the pool as separate from valuation
Accepting a top-up at every round without question

columns.label: What wins ground
points: A named hiring plan with grants role by role
"8% covers 18 months, and we will top up at Series A when you know more"
Offering a smaller pool now with an agreed top-up mechanism later
Comparing offers on effective price per share, not headline valuation
Asking that any top-up be shared, not loaded entirely pre-money

body.label: Unallocated pool shares are not free
body.value: They dilute you whether or not anyone gets them
body.context: On a fully diluted basis the whole pool counts from day one. A 15% pool of which only 6% is ever granted means 9% of the company sat idle, having already diluted the founders, until it is returned or reused in a later round.

children.text: What the Pool Means for Employees

body.title: The life of one employee's ESOP grant

events.title: Grant
events.description: The employee receives a grant letter: a number of options, an exercise price and a vesting schedule. Nothing is owned yet, and the options cannot be sold.

events.title: Cliff
events.description: The first 25% typically vests on completing one year. Leave before this and the entire grant lapses.

events.title: Vesting continues
events.description: The rest vests monthly or quarterly over the remaining three years, so the full grant is earned at the end of year four.

events.title: Options become shares
events.description: The employee pays the exercise price and receives actual shares. In India this is when a tax liability normally arises on the difference between fair value and exercise price, subject to a deferral available to eligible startups.

events.title: Shares become money
events.description: Only when the company is acquired, lists, or runs a buyback do the shares turn into cash. Until then the value is on paper.

body.text: The hardest part of Indian ESOPs is the gap between owning shares and having money. An employee can face a tax bill at exercise on a valuation nobody can sell into. This is why serious companies run periodic ESOP buybacks, as Flipkart has done in several widely reported rounds, and why a grant letter that never leads to a liquidity event buys goodwill only once.

body.title: How ESOPs are taxed in India, in plain terms

children.text: There are two taxable moments, and founders should be able to explain both to their team.
At exercise:
the difference between the fair market value of the share and the price the employee pays is treated as a perquisite, taxed as salary income, with the employer responsible for withholding.
At sale:
any gain above that fair market value is a capital gain, taxed according to how long the shares were held and whether the company is listed.

Eligible DPIIT-recognised startups can defer the tax withholding at exercise for a specified period, which exists precisely because employees were being taxed on paper gains they could not monetise. The deferral is narrow: it applies only to startups holding the relevant certificate. Section references have changed with the new income tax legislation, so confirm the current provisions, rates and holding periods with a tax adviser before communicating anything to your team.

body.title: Who pays for the pool?
body.question: A term sheet says a 12% option pool will be created pre-money, alongside an investment buying 20% of the company. Who bears the dilution from the pool?
options: The new investor, because they asked for it
The existing shareholders, mainly the founders
The new investor and existing shareholders in proportion to their stakes
Nobody, because unissued options do not count until they are granted
body.explanation: A pre-money pool is carved out before the new money arrives, so it comes entirely out of existing holders' shares. The investor's 20% is protected. If the pool were created post-money, the dilution would be shared, and on a fully diluted basis the pool counts even before options are granted.

body.title: Size the pool from the plan
body.prompt: A founder plans to grant 1.5% to a VP Engineering, 1% to a Head of Sales, 0.4% each to four senior engineers, 0.15% each to twelve mid-level hires, and wants a 1.3% buffer. What total pool does the plan justify, in percent?
body.explanation: 1.5 + 1.0 + (4 × 0.4 = 1.6) + (12 × 0.15 = 1.8) + 1.3 = 7.2%. Walking an investor through this table is a far stronger negotiation than calling 15% unfair, and each percentage point saved is worth real money at the post-money valuation.

body.title: The pool that ate the raise
body.scenario:
Nikhil's Noida logistics startup has 50,00,000 shares held by three founders. He has two term sheets for ₹10 crore.
Offer A: ₹40 crore pre-money, 15% ESOP pool created pre-money.
Offer B: ₹36 crore pre-money, 8% ESOP pool created pre-money.
His honest 18-month hiring plan needs about 7%.
body.prompt: Which offer leaves the founders owning more, and what should Nikhil do next?
body.modelAnswer:
Work out the founders' ending stake in each case.
Offer A: post-money is ₹50 crore, so the investor takes ₹10 ÷ ₹50 = 20%. The 15% pool is carved out pre-money, so the founders keep 100% − 20% − 15% = 65% of the company.
Offer B: post-money is ₹46 crore, so the investor takes ₹10 ÷ ₹46 = 21.7%. The 8% pool comes pre-money, leaving the founders 100% − 21.7% − 8% = 70.3%.
Offer B wins on ownership by about 5.3 percentage points, despite a headline valuation ₹4 crore lower. Check the value too: 70.3% of ₹46 crore is about ₹32.3 crore, against 65% of ₹50 crore, which is ₹32.5 crore. The paper values are nearly identical, so the real difference is that Offer A's bigger pool means more of the company has already been promised away, while Offer B leaves room to grant thoughtfully.
What Nikhil should do: go back to Offer A with the hiring plan and ask for the pool at 8%, pointing out that the plan needs 7% with a buffer. If they hold at 15%, ask for the excess to be created post-money so the dilution is shared. Compare final offers on price per share and on founder ownership after the pool, not on the pre-money number. And agree now how top-ups will be handled at the Series A, because that negotiation is far harder later.

body.title: Where the cost lands
body.textWithBlank: When an option pool is created ___-money, the dilution falls entirely on existing shareholders and the new investor's percentage is untouched.
body.explanation: A pre-money pool is carved out before the investment, so it reduces the effective price the investor pays. A post-money pool dilutes everyone, including the new investor.

cards.definition: Shares reserved for employee grants, approved by the board and shareholders and administered under a written plan.
A share count including all issued shares, the entire option pool granted or not, and all convertible instruments.
A pool created before the investment, so existing shareholders alone bear the dilution.
Price per share multiplied by pre-round shares: what the founders are really paid, after the pool is carved out.
The amount an employee pays to convert vested options into actual shares.
An increase in the pool at a later round, usually created pre-money again unless negotiated otherwise.
A company-run purchase of employee shares, often the only way employees convert vested equity into cash before an exit.

points: A pre-money option pool is carved out of existing shareholders, so the founders pay for it and the investor's percentage is untouched.
It quietly cuts the price: ₹20 crore pre-money with a 10% pre-money pool is an effective pre-money of ₹17.5 crore.
Compare offers on price per share and on founder ownership after the pool, never on the headline valuation.
Negotiate pool size with a bottom-up hiring plan. A plan needing 7% beats an argument about what is standard.
Unallocated pool shares dilute you from day one, because investors measure everything fully diluted.
For employees, options pass through grant, cliff, vesting, exercise and only then a liquidity event. Tax usually arises at exercise, with a narrow deferral for eligible startups.
Agree how pool top-ups will work at the next round while you still have leverage.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. ESOP taxation, the startup deferral and company law approval requirements change, and section references have shifted with the new income tax legislation. Verify current provisions with a qualified tax adviser or company secretary before granting options or communicating tax treatment to employees. The Chennai and Noida companies and all figures are illustrative.
